report:
## Conclusion

For the general population, taking vitamin C regularly does **not prevent colds**. Across over 29 trials with more than 11,000 participants, the Cochrane systematic review found no reduction in cold incidence with routine supplementation ([Cochrane, PMC8078152](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8078152/); [NCBI Bookshelf](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279544/)).

However, vitamin C does have a modest effect on cold **duration and severity** when taken regularly (not just after symptoms start): duration was reduced by about 8% in adults and 14% in children ([Cochrane](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD000980_vitamin-c-preventing-and-treating-common-cold)), and a 2023 meta-analysis found a ~15% reduction in symptom severity with ≥1 g/day ([BMC Public Health](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12889-023-17229-8)). Once a cold has already started, beginning vitamin C at that point shows little to no benefit.

An important exception exists for people under brief but intense physical/environmental stress—marathon runners, skiers, soldiers in subarctic conditions. In these groups, regular vitamin C supplementation roughly halved the incidence of colds (pooled RR ~0.50) ([PMC8078152](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8078152/); [JACI](https://www.jacionline.org/article/S0091-6749(08)01743-0/fulltext)).

**Bottom line:** For most healthy people, daily vitamin C is unlikely to stop you from catching colds, though it may slightly shorten how long a cold lasts and how bad symptoms feel. It's more clearly useful for people undergoing short bursts of extreme physical exertion or cold exposure, where it can meaningfully cut cold risk. High-dose vitamin C is generally safe at commonly used doses (1–2 g/day), so trying it carries low risk even if the average benefit is small.
